title: Bootcamp
author: Joe Kirby
summary: At Michaela Community School, new Year 7 pupils spend seven days in Bootcamp — a structured pre-term induction designed to replace ingrained bad habits with the mindset and routines needed to succeed at secondary school. Rather than a rushed single-day induction where new students are subject to bullying by older peers, Bootcamp dedicates a full week to teaching explicit routines (entering a classroom in under 30 seconds, handing out books in 5 seconds), school philosophy (stoicism via Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, and Epictetus), and the logic behind Michaela’s unusually high standards. Kirby argues that once pupils understand why the rules exist — because teachers believe in them and want them to succeed — they willingly embrace those standards and begin to feel empowered rather than repressed. The experience of watching pupils raise their standards in real time, enjoying the challenge of beating their own classroom-entry records, illustrates how transparency about purpose transforms compliance into intrinsic motivation. Bootcamp also proves transformative for new teachers, who are inducted into the school’s culture at the same time as Year 7 pupils, enabling them to begin with maximum authority and earn the respect of older pupils quickly. The article presents Bootcamp as a frontloading strategy: by building a shared repository of values, virtues, stories, and mantras in the first seven days, Michaela gives both pupils and staff a foundation that pays compound returns across a seven-year secondary career.
points: Michaela’s Bootcamp replaces chaotic single-day inductions with a deliberate seven-day programme that teaches routines, school philosophy, and the reasoning behind every rule before older pupils arrive — eliminating the bullying and intimidation that typically marks Year 7 inductions.

By frontloading explicit instruction in classroom entry, demerit response, and emotional self-regulation (drawing on Stoic philosophy), Bootcamp aims to replace years of ingrained bad habits in the first week rather than fighting them incrementally all year.

Pupils accept demanding standards more readily once they understand the reasoning — that high expectations reflect care and belief, not power or punishment — suggesting that transparency about the ‘why’ behind rules is itself a powerful behaviour-change lever.

Stoicism features prominently as a philosophical framework, offering pupils a language for self-regulation: ‘it’s not events, but our judgments that disturb us’ is taught as a practical life tool rather than abstract philosophy, particularly for pupils who have been exposed to environments dominated by blame and excuses.

Bootcamp functions simultaneously as new-teacher induction: starting without older pupils allows new staff to establish authority, practise routines, and internalise school culture before the full cohort arrives, giving them maximum confidence and credibility from day one.
quotes: At Michaela, we take the most time for our youngest pupils, with 7 days to set them up to succeed in their first steps on the start of their seven-year journey at secondary school – without any older pupils there at all. We recognise that they have to navigate the new demands of some 10 different teachers, and 120 pupils in their year group, very different to their primary schools, where they tend to have one form teacher all year and sometimes only 50 children in their year group. Bootcamp gives the new kids seven days to adjust these new challenges and rise to our high standards.

We teach them all our school rules, the consequences that follow from making wise choices, and the consequences that follow from making unwise choices. We explain in minute detail what we give demerits for and what we give detentions for. We clarify precisely how to avoid detentions.

We tell our pupils that the reason their teachers at Michaela are so strict and so tough on them is because they care about them so much, because they believe in them so much, and because they love seeing them succeed and improve and achieve. It is our intention that this positivity, warmth, care and tough love pervades every interaction we have with pupils in school, even when we are disciplining them.

When we started in 2014 with our first bootcamp, I thought its major advantage was that it changed pupils’ habits. By 2016, now that we have run bootcamp three times, I’ve seen that there is another, equally important advantage: not only is it life-changing for new pupils, it is a game-changer for new teachers, too. Reading the blogposts of our new teachers Mike Taylor and Hin Tai Ting, demonstrate that new teachers are able to start with maximum authority, certainty and confidence so that they swiftly earn the respect of the older pupils they teach.
